definition:
The image of God (in Latin, imago Dei) is the Bible's name for what makes human beings unique among God's creatures: God made them to reflect him, to represent him in the world, and to live in relationship with him. Genesis says it once at the Bible's opening and then lets the rest of Scripture fill it in. Christians have located the image in different places, in human reason and moral capacity, in the royal calling to rule the earth on God's behalf, in the relationships of love for which people are made, or in some combination of these. Whatever else it is, it grounds the worth of every human being, it survives the fall, and in the New Testament it is centered on Jesus Christ, who is himself the image of God and into whose likeness believers are being renewed.

Two Hebrew words carry the idea. Tselem, ‘image’, appears fewer than twenty times in the Hebrew Bible, and most of its uses outside Genesis are concrete: carved or cast images of false gods (Numbers 33:52, Amos 5:26), models of tumors and rats (1 Samuel 6:5), and, in the Aramaic of Daniel 3, Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue. It can also mean a passing shadow (Psalm 39:6). Demut, ‘likeness’, means resemblance or pattern; it is used of the model of an altar Ahaz sent from Damascus (2 Kings 16:10) and over and over in Ezekiel's vision, where the prophet can only speak of ‘the likeness of’ what he sees. In Genesis 1:26 the two words overlap heavily, and Genesis itself uses them interchangeably (5:1 has only ‘likeness’, 9:6 only ‘image’, 5:3 reverses the order). A statue found in 1979 at Tell Fekheriye in Syria, from the ninth century BC, carries an Akkadian and Aramaic inscription that uses the Aramaic cognates of both words for the same royal statue. The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, rendered them eikōn and homoiōsis. In the New Testament eikōn, ‘image’, appears about two dozen times, of Caesar's face on a coin, of idols, and above all of Christ; Hebrews 1:3 adds charaktēr, the ‘exact imprint’ a seal leaves in wax.
ot:
The phrase appears at the climax of the creation account. After six days of making and ordering, God speaks in a new way: “Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness, to rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air” (Genesis 1:26). The plural has been read as a plural of majesty, as God addressing his heavenly council, as God deliberating with himself, or, by the church fathers, as a first glimpse of the Trinity. The next verse is poetry: “So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). Three things are tied to the image in the text. It belongs to humanity as a whole, male and female together. It is linked at once to rule over the creatures, the Hebrew radah, a word used elsewhere of kings. And it is followed by blessing and the commission to “fill the earth and subdue it” (Genesis 1:28). The Hebrew preposition in ‘in our image’ can also be read ‘as our image’, and D. J. A. Clines argued in 1968 that humanity does not merely contain the image but is God's image in the world.

The ancient setting sharpens the point. In Egypt and Mesopotamia a king could be called the image of a god: the Egyptian royal name Tutankhamun means ‘living image of Amun’, and Assyrian court letters could call the king the image of a god. Temples housed cult statues, also called images, through which a god was believed to be present and to act. Genesis says something startling against that background. Every human being, not only the king, is God's image, and the only image God places in his world is a living person. That is why Israel was forbidden to make images of God (Exodus 20:4). At Horeb they “saw no form of any kind,” so they must not make an idol “in the likeness of a male or female” (Deuteronomy 4:15-16). God already had an image on earth; to carve another was to insult both God and the human beings who bear it. Catherine McDowell, in The Image of God in the Garden of Eden (2015), argued that the account of Adam's making in Genesis 2 echoes the Mesopotamian and Egyptian rituals for making and animating a cult statue, and that image language in Genesis is also the language of kinship. Genesis 5 supports that second point: God made Adam “in His own likeness,” and Adam “had a son in his own likeness, after his own image” (Genesis 5:1-3). To be God's image is something like being his child, which is why Luke's genealogy ends, “the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38).

The image survives the fall. The serpent's temptation was to “be like God” (Genesis 3:5), a grasping after what humanity already had as a gift. After the flood, when violence had filled the earth, God still grounds the prohibition of murder in the image: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man his blood will be shed; for in His own image God has made mankind” (Genesis 9:6). The image is the reason a human life cannot be taken as an animal's can, even in a world corrupted by sin. Psalm 8 celebrates the same dignity without using the word. Looking at the heavens, the psalmist asks, “what is man that You are mindful of him,” and answers, “You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor. You made him ruler of the works of Your hands” (Psalm 8:4-6). The word rendered ‘angels’ is elohim, which can mean God or heavenly beings, and the Septuagint's ‘angels’ is the reading Hebrews later quotes.

The prophets approach the image from the other side, through idolatry. Isaiah mocks the craftsman who “fashions it in the likeness of man, like man in all his glory, that it may dwell in a shrine” (Isaiah 44:13), and asks, “To whom will you liken God? To what image will you compare Him?” (Isaiah 40:18). The psalmist warns that idol-makers “become like them” (Psalm 115:8): human beings reflect whatever they worship. Ezekiel's vision of God's throne reaches its height with “a figure like that of a man,” which the prophet calls “the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD” (Ezekiel 1:26-28), and Daniel sees beasts ruling the nations until “One like the Son of Man” receives “dominion, glory, and kingship” (Daniel 7:13-14). The human form belongs close to God's own glory, and the rule given to humanity in Genesis is restored in a human figure. Jewish writing before Christ carried the theme further. The Wisdom of Solomon, probably from the first century BC, says God made humans for incorruption as an image of his own eternity, and Philo of Alexandria, early in the first century AD, located the image in the human mind.
nt:
The New Testament's decisive move is to name Jesus as the image of God. Paul speaks of “the glory of Christ, who is the image of God” (2 Corinthians 4:4), and says God has given “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6), words that deliberately recall the first day of creation. The Colossian hymn begins, “The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation” (Colossians 1:15). Hebrews calls the Son “the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature” (Hebrews 1:3), and in John's Gospel Jesus says, “Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). These texts claim more than that Jesus is a good example of humanity in God's image. He is the image in the full sense, the one in whom the invisible God is seen, because “the one and only Son, who is Himself God” has made him known (John 1:18). Paul also calls Adam “a pattern of the One to come” (Romans 5:14) and names Christ the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45), the one who completes what the first man failed to be. Many readers have seen a deliberate contrast in Philippians 2:6-7: where Adam grasped at being like God, Christ, “existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped,” but took “the form of a servant.”

Hebrews reads Psalm 8 through Jesus. It admits that “at present we do not see everything subject to him,” that is, to humanity; “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death” (Hebrews 2:8-9). The royal calling of the image, left unfinished by Adam's children, is fulfilled by the one who took the lowest place. Salvation is then described as being remade in his likeness. God predestined his people “to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). This is a present process: believers “are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18). It touches the mind and conduct: the new self “is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator” (Colossians 3:10) and is “created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness” (Ephesians 4:24). It will be completed at the resurrection: “just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man” (1 Corinthians 15:49), and “when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2).

The renewal has social edges. Right after speaking of the image of the Creator, Colossians adds, “Here there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free, but Christ is all and is in all” (Colossians 3:11). The image also still governs how everyone is treated, believer or not. James condemns the tongue that blesses God and curses “men, who have been made in God’s likeness” (James 3:9); even after the fall, people bear enough of God's likeness that to curse them is to dishonor him. Paul tells the Athenians that humans are God's offspring and therefore must not imagine God to be “like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man’s skill and imagination” (Acts 17:29), and he describes sin as having “exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles” (Romans 1:23), the reverse of Genesis 1. In 1 Corinthians 11:7 Paul calls the man “the image and glory of God” in an argument about head coverings; interpreters differ over whether he is drawing on Genesis 2's order of creation or limiting the image, and Genesis 1:27 explicitly includes the woman. When Jesus is shown a coin and asks, “Whose image is this?” (Matthew 22:20), he does not spell out the point, but readers have long noticed that if Caesar may claim what bears his image, God claims what bears his. The canon ends with a counterfeit image, the image of the beast that demands worship (Revelation 13:14-15), and with the true image restored in a city where God's servants “will see His face” (Revelation 22:4).

keyTexts.why: The founding text: humanity, male and female, is made in God's image and likeness, blessed, and given rule over the creatures.
Adam bears God's likeness and Seth bears Adam's likeness and image, showing that image language is also the language of sonship and that the image continues after the fall.
After the flood, murder is forbidden because humans are made in God's image, so the image survives sin and grounds the value of every life.
Israel saw no form at Horeb and must make no image of God in human or animal likeness, which sets the prohibition of idols beside the truth that God has already placed his living image in the world.
The psalmist marvels that small humanity is crowned with glory and honor and set over God's works, the image's royal dignity in poetry.
The idol-maker carves a god in human likeness, a satire that shows what happens when human beings turn the image on its head.
God's purpose for his people is that they be conformed to the image of his Son, the firstborn among many brothers.
Christ is the last Adam, and believers who have borne the earthly man's likeness will bear the heavenly man's likeness at the resurrection.
Beholding the Lord's glory, believers are being transformed into his image by the Spirit, a present and gradual renewal.
Christ is the image of God, and the light of God's glory is seen in his face, words that recall creation's first light.
The Son is the image of the invisible God, the heading under which the New Testament gathers the whole doctrine.
The new self is renewed in knowledge after the image of its Creator, in a community where ethnic and social divisions no longer rule.
Psalm 8's promise of human rule is not yet seen in humanity at large but is seen in Jesus, crowned after suffering death.
Cursing any person is incompatible with blessing God, because people are made in his likeness, even now.

history:
The early church read the image through Christ. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies, about 180) taught that humanity was made according to the image of the Son and that Christ, recapitulating Adam's history, restored what Adam lost; in book 5 he distinguished the image, which all humans possess, from the likeness, a gift of the Spirit lost in the fall and restored in Christ. The Alexandrian theologians, Clement and Origen, stressed that the Word himself is the Image of God and that humans were made ‘according to the image’, as an image of the Image. Athanasius, in On the Incarnation (dated by scholars from about 318 to the 330s), compared humanity to a portrait defaced by sin and said the Word came in person so that the portrait could be restored from the original sitting for it again. Augustine's On the Trinity (completed about 420) found a reflection of the Trinity in the human mind's memory, understanding, and will, most fully when the mind remembers, knows, and loves God. John of Damascus, in the eighth century, took the image to mean reason and free will and the likeness to mean likeness in virtue, a distinction many Eastern theologians kept and connected to theosis, the believer's growing participation in the life of God. In the controversy over icons John also argued that because the invisible God became visible in Christ, Christ may be depicted, and the Second Council of Nicaea (787) agreed.

Medieval theology built on Augustine. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I, question 93) placed the image in humanity's rational nature and distinguished three degrees of it: the natural capacity to know and love God, which all have; its actual conformity to God by grace, in the righteous; and its perfection in glory. The Reformers read the image more in terms of relationship and righteousness. Luther, in his Lectures on Genesis (from 1535), set aside the distinction between image and likeness and identified the image with the original righteousness lost in the fall, to be restored through the gospel. Calvin (Institutes 1.15, final edition 1559) held that the image shines chiefly in the soul but extends to the whole person, and that after the fall it was not wholly destroyed but so corrupted that what remains is deformed. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, question 6) says God created humans good and in his image, in true righteousness and holiness, and the Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647, question 10) speaks of knowledge, righteousness, and holiness, with dominion over the creatures, drawing its words from Colossians 3:10 and Ephesians 4:24.

Modern theology has pursued several lines at once. Herman Bavinck, in his Reformed Dogmatics (first published 1895 to 1901), insisted that a human being does not merely have or bear the image but is the image, body and soul together. In 1934 Emil Brunner and Karl Barth quarreled over natural theology; Brunner held that a formal image, humanity's responsibility before God, survives the fall while the material image, right relationship with God, was lost. Barth, in Church Dogmatics III/1 (1945), read the image as relationship, humanity as male and female reflecting the relational life of God. Old Testament scholars such as Gerhard von Rad and D. J. A. Clines (1968) emphasized the royal and representative sense drawn from the ancient Near East, which J. Richard Middleton developed in The Liberating Image (2005) and Catherine McDowell extended toward kinship in 2015. The Second Vatican Council's Gaudium et Spes (1965) taught that the mystery of humanity becomes clear only in the mystery of the incarnate Word. John Kilner's Dignity and Destiny (2015) argued that Scripture never says the image is damaged, and that it names both a status every person already has and a destiny fulfilled in Christ. Christian thinking on slavery, race, disability, the unborn, and the dying has repeatedly turned on this doctrine; the fuller survey of Christian views of the human person is at /theology/doctrine/anthropology, and the study on humanity in this Study Bible sets the image within the whole doctrine of human nature.

differ.body: The image is something humans are and have: reason, moral awareness, freedom, and the capacity to know God. This is the view of much of the church's history, from the Alexandrians and Augustine to Aquinas. Its defenders point out that rule over creation, relationship with God, and moral responsibility all require a certain kind of creature, one who can understand, choose, and love, and that Scripture's renewal of the image ‘in knowledge’ (Colossians 3:10) fits a view that gives the mind a central place. They add that capacities belong to human nature as such, not to each individual's present performance, so that an infant or a person with severe disability is fully human and fully in the image.

The image is a vocation: humanity is God's representative, set in the world to rule it on his behalf as a king's statue marks his reign. Its defenders, among them Gerhard von Rad, D. J. A. Clines, and J. Richard Middleton, argue that this is what the words meant in their ancient setting, where kings were called images of gods, and that Genesis 1:26 ties the image directly to rule. Genesis gives the royal status to every human being, not to kings alone, and Psalm 8, Daniel 7, and Hebrews 2 trace that calling until it is fulfilled in Jesus. The view stresses stewardship of the earth and the dignity of ordinary work.

The image is found in relationship: with God, with one another, and especially in humanity as male and female. Karl Barth and many after him argued that Genesis 1:27 explains the image by the words ‘male and female He created them’, and that a God who is Father, Son, and Spirit is reflected in creatures made for communion. Defenders note that the image is lost or regained in Scripture in ways that concern relationship with God, that the New Testament speaks of it in terms of love and community (Colossians 3:10-11), and that the view guards against defining human worth by ability.

The image is first of all Christ, and human beings are made according to that image and destined to be conformed to it. Defenders, from Irenaeus to modern writers such as John Kilner and Stanley Grenz, argue that the New Testament applies ‘image’ almost entirely to Christ and to believers being renewed in him, so the doctrine should be read from its end rather than its beginning. The image is a status every person already holds before God, which is why it is not damaged by sin, and a destiny fulfilled in union with Christ. Many who hold this view combine it with elements of the others, since the Christ who is the image also reasons, rules, and loves.

errors:
The church has rejected any teaching that denies the image to some human beings. Arguments that Africans or Indigenous peoples lacked full humanity, used to defend slavery and conquest, and later arguments for eugenics that ranked human lives by fitness, all contradict Genesis 1:27 and 9:6; the church's own record here is full of failure, and the doctrine has been the strongest argument against it. A related error ties the image so closely to present abilities (intelligence, speech, productivity) that the unborn, the severely disabled, or those with dementia seem to have less of it. Scripture grounds the image in God's act of creation, not in any person's performance.

Other errors misread the text. In the fourth century some Christians, sometimes called anthropomorphites, took Genesis 1:26 to mean that God has a human body, a view the church rejected because God is spirit and invisible (John 4:24, Colossians 1:15). Gnostic teachers treated the image as a divine spark trapped in matter, despising the body God made and calls good. Some have read Paul in 1 Corinthians 11:7 as denying the image to women, which Genesis 1:27 rules out. Some have treated dominion as license to exploit the earth, a charge the historian Lynn White pressed in a 1967 essay; Genesis 2:15 sets that rule in the language of cultivating and keeping a garden. And some have spoken as though the fall erased the image entirely, which Genesis 9:6 and James 3:9 deny.
life:
The image of God changes how a person looks at every other person. The stranger, the enemy, the child who cannot yet speak, and the elderly neighbor who can no longer remember are each God's image, so that contempt, cursing, and violence toward them are offenses against God himself. James draws the practical line at the tongue: the same mouth cannot bless God and curse the people who bear his likeness. It also changes how a person looks at himself or herself. Human worth is not earned by achievement or lost by failure, illness, or age; it is given, and it cannot be taken away by anyone's opinion.

The doctrine also gives the Christian life its direction. If Christ is the image and believers are being conformed to him, holiness is not a set of rules added to human nature but the recovery of what humanity was made to be. That renewal happens slowly, as believers behold Christ's glory in the Scriptures, in worship, and in one another, and it will be complete only when they see him. Prayer, work, and the care of creation become the ordinary ways God's image lives out its calling, and the hope of the resurrection is the hope of finally being fully human.
questions: Genesis 9:6 and James 3:9 say that people still bear God's image after the fall. How should that shape the way you speak about people you disagree with or find hard to love?
Of the four ways of understanding the image (capacity, calling, relationship, and conformity to Christ), which seems strongest to you from the texts, and what might the others add?
Paul says believers are being transformed into Christ's image by beholding his glory. What does beholding Christ look like in an ordinary week?
